transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-11-04 15:30 PT | Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Leah (Redwood SE - runtime), Marco (Redwood - networking), Marta (Clairvoyant Head ML Infra), Ravi (Clairvoyant Cloud Architect), Priya (Clairvoyant Security)

[00:00] Samir: Hey team, thanks for joining. The goal for today is to walk through private VPC networking options for Redwood Private and then deep dive into runtime perf tradeoffs - batching, KV cache, quantization, etc. We'll surface any blockers for the pilot.
[00:18] Marta: Hi all, thanks, quick context - we're moving inference for our customer-facing product into our VPC; we need predictable latency and strict data residency. Security will require KMS integration, audit logs, and our SSO. We're evaluating PrivateLink vs just letting Redwood egress through NAT.
[00:35] Leah: Great, that's exactly what we wanted to cover. I'll start with a high level on how Redwood Private sits in a customer VPC, then Marco can cover the networking specifics. Quick question for Ravi: what's your preferred cloud?
[00:45] Ravi: We're mostly on AWS, some accounts in GCP but this pilot will run in our primary AWS account. We have existing transit gateway and use Direct Connect for on-prem connectivity.
[00:55] Marco: OK AWS is good, we have a couple common patterns: PrivateLink endpoints for control plane and model artifact pulls, plus optional NAT egress for non-sensitive telemetry; or full egress via PrivateLink with VPC endpoints to avoid NAT altogether. We'll walk pros/cons.
[01:12] Priya: From security, PrivateLink is preferred since it avoids public IPs for control plane comms. We also need to know where logs and metrics go — can they be kept in our account?
[01:25] Samir: Short answer: yes, Redwood Private can be deployed so that metrics and logs are pushed to your accounts or routed to your S3/Kinesis endpoints; audit logs from the control plane can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll share detailed log flows.
[01:40] Leah: On runtime, important piece is the KV cache and prefix caching. If your inference hosts are inside your VPC and run the Redwood runtime locally, the KV cache sits in-process or in a local LRU cache on the node. That means requests don't round-trip to an external cache for each token - huge latency win.
[01:58] Ravi: Wait, are we running the model weights in our VPC? Or are you hosting a control plane with model variants on Redwood side?
[02:10] Leah: For Private, you can do hybrid. The control plane (orchestrator) can be in Redwood control plane or a customer-managed control plane. For artifact hosting, you can pull model weights from your S3 (private) or from Redwood's storage via PrivateLink. In the pilot we typically stage weights in a customer S3 bucket to meet residency requirements.
[02:30] Marta: Good. On perf: our SLAs need p95 < 200ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens) and throughput of ~120 concurrent qps. How feasible on H100s?
[02:45] Leah: For short seqs ~128, H100 with quantization and good batching can hit p95 in the 80-150ms range depending on batching and KV cache hit rate. The catch: KV cache warmup is critical for long-running chat sessions. If cache miss rate is high, first-token latency spikes because of KV cache fill ops.
[03:05] Marco: On networking, if you do PrivateLink for model artifact pulls, you'll avoid NAT egress and firewall rules; but PrivateLink requires ENIs in your subnets and cross-account endpoint configuration. NAT path is easier to get started but you need to manage egress IPs and routing, and some customers prefer no NAT for compliance.
[03:28] Ravi: How about throughput when we do batching? Our app has bursty traffic; can autoscaling handle batch size increases without hurting latency for tails?
[03:40] Leah: We have continuous batching in the runtime that aggregates small requests into micro-batches dynamically. For bursty workloads we recommend a hybrid: small concurrency headroom plus adaptive batching. You can set a latency SLO and the runtime will bound max batch timeout, so latency SLO is honored at cost of lower throughput.
[03:58] Marta: Can you explain quantization impacts? We want cost savings but worried about quality regressions.
[04:10] Leah: Sure. We support 8-bit and 4-bit quantization profiles. For many decoder-only models, Q4_INT8 gives 2-4x throughput improvements with minor quality drop on average. We run evals on your prompts — we'll recommend a quantization profile per workload. For safety-critical responses you can pin certain model versions to float 16 or BF16.
[04:35] Priya: KMS — where are encryption keys held? We need customer-managed keys (CMKs).
[04:45] Samir: Redwood Private supports integration with your KMS/HSM. You can bring your own CMKs in your account and we can encrypt model artifacts at rest and TLS certs are issued via your CA if needed. We'll include KMS integration steps in the security docs.
[05:05] [05:05] Marco: Back to DNS — important gotcha: when you create PrivateLink endpoints, they create interface ENIs and often a private hosted zone mapping the service name to the endpoint IPs. If you use Route53 private hosted zones elsewhere, ensure there's no name collision; also confirm resolver rules if you have split-horizon DNS.
[05:25] Ravi: We're running internal resolver and outbound DNS forwarding to on-prem. Any special config?
[05:32] Marco: Use conditional forwarders or Route53 resolver rules for the Redwood control plane domains. If you choose full PrivateLink (no public egress), make sure the service discovery names resolve to the interface endpoints in each subnet.
[05:46] Leah: On cache architecture: we recommend colocating model runtime and KV cache on the same subnet for minimal intra-VPC latency. For multi-AZ resilience, we peer subnets or use a multi-AZ cache replication strategy. But cross-AZ traffic can add 1-3ms depending on region.
[06:05] Marta: Do you recommend using Elastic Fabric Adapter or any special NICs for performance?
[06:12] Leah: For high throughput (hundreds of tokens/sec) we see gains from enhanced networking, EFA for HPC-like workloads helps distributed inference when you shard across nodes. For single-node GPU inference EFA isn't necessary; ensure instance types have good throughput to the GPU (i.e., A100/H100 family).
[06:30] Ravi: Example network design — do you expect us to open inbound ports? Or is the runtime inbound-only via PrivateLink?
[06:38] Marco: PrivateLink avoids opening inbound to instances. The interface endpoint accepts traffic from our control plane to your endpoint; if you run the runtime in your VPC the control plane can orchestrate jobs via PrivateLink. For customer-hosted workloads, we rely on IAM roles and signed mTLS sessions; no wide-open inbound allowed.
[06:56] Priya: Audit logs — can we get request-level logs with redaction? We need PII stripped before logs leave our account.
[07:06] Samir: Yes, logs can be configured to redact or only emit aggregated metrics. We can also route raw audit logs to your S3 and you can run your own ETL. We'll document fields and redaction knobs.
[07:22] [07:22] Customer: cool, what's the pilot scope?
[07:26] Leah: Pilot: 1) deploy Redwood runtime in one private subnet; 2) stage model artifacts in your S3; 3) use PrivateLink endpoints for control plane and artifact pulls; 4) run benchmark suite (H100, batch sizes 1,4,8,16, seq len 128/512/1024), measure p50/p95/p99 and token/sec; 5) evaluate quantization profile and KV cache hit rate.
[07:52] Ravi: Sounds good. For the benchmarking, what telemetry do you need from our side?
[07:58] Leah: We need kube/pod metrics (if k8s), network egress metrics, GPU utilization, and sample prompt sets. We'll provide a spreadsheet with canonical tests.
[08:12] Marta: Any limitations around private hosted zones and certificate issuance?
[08:18] Marco: Certs for PrivateLink endpoints can use ACM Private CA or you can bring certs. If you have CA constraints we can integrate as well. Just call out the CN names you need in the diagram.
[08:30] [08:30] Transcript continues with technical back-and-forth...
[12:45] Leah: A couple of subtle perf points — KV cache eviction policy and cache warming: when you spin up new pods, they start cold; if you have long-running chat sessions consider sticky sessions or a session routing layer to preserved warmed KV cache on the same node. We do session affinity as an option.
[13:05] Marta: How does batching interact with affinity? If we route to same node for affinity and same session we might reduce batching opportunities?
[13:15] Leah: Correct, there's a tradeoff: affinity increases hit rate but reduces cross-session batching. Our runtime uses micro-batching within the session and also opportunistic cross-session batching with a bounded timeout. You can tune batch windows per route.
[13:30] Ravi: For model updates how are rollouts handled in Private? Canary in our VPC?
[13:38] Samir: Yes, canary within your VPC is standard. We support model version pinning per route and progressive traffic shifting. Rollouts use in-VPC health checks; if a new model increases latency beyond SLOs we automatically fallback to previous version.
[13:55] Priya: What about data plane encryption for KV cache in-memory?
[14:02] Leah: In-memory caches are not encrypted at rest (they're RAM). For disk-backed caches we encrypt using your CMKs. In transit we use mTLS and customer TLS certs for any inter-service RPC.
[14:18] Marco: On IP addressing: plan for ENI IP exhaustion if you create many interface endpoints in small subnets. Each PrivateLink endpoint adds ENIs (one per AZ), and each ENI consumes IPs from the subnet. So choose subnet sizes accordingly.
[14:36] Ravi: Good callout. We'll share our subnet CIDRs.
[14:40] Marta: Any experience with bursty traffic patterns and cold start penalties?
[14:47] Leah: Cold starts are mainly weight load time and KV cache misses. For large models with bigger weights, we recommend pre-warming a fraction of nodes and using a small cluster that stays up for the busiest hours. Also consider quantized weights that reduce load time.
[15:05] Samir: Let's cover metrics we'll collect in the pilot: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (requests/sec and tokens/sec), GPU utilization, cache hit/miss ratio, model artifact pull time, and network egress volumes. We'll add SLO checks and synthetic tests.
[15:28] Ravi: Can we limit telemetry that leaves the VPC? We only want aggregated metrics out.
[15:34] Samir: Absolutely — we can flip a switch to only emit aggregates and route raw traces to your S3 for internal analysis.
[15:42] [15:42] Marco: Quick note on DNS TTL for PrivateLink — if you rely on DNS for endpoint failover, the TTL should be low so new IPs are picked up quickly for endpoint failover, but low TTL increases resolver traffic. Balance per your ops.
[15:58] Marta: OK, recap and next steps?
[16:02] Samir: Recap: Redwood to share PrivateLink/Terraform example, VPC diagram, and benchmark plan. Leah to prepare the benchmark spreadsheet and KV cache config. Customer to share subnet CIDRs, SAML metadata and designate security contact. We'll aim to kick off pilot next week.
[16:20] Priya: We'll get SAML and the questionnaire over; note we'll want a SOC2 addendum in the contract.
[16:27] Samir: Noted, we'll push the SSO/KMS/SOC2 docs.
[16:32] Marta: Thanks everyone.
[16:35] [16:35] Call ends.

Notes on transcription: some speaker labels were aggregated, minor mis-transcriptions of product names (e.g., 'Private Link' vs 'PrivateLink'), and occasional dropped filler words — original audio quality medium.
